Spend the next two hours testing the concrete batching change to C on the representative workload, including durable acknowledgement under batching. The potential benefit is meeting both hard requirements with the existing adapter and less maintenance; the available time permits this test while retaining A as a qualified fallback. C’s improvement is a hypothesis, not a result.

A is the only currently demonstrated qualifying choice: durability passes and representative p99 is 62 ms. If commitment must happen immediately, choose A. Otherwise, commit now to the bounded C experiment and defer final selection until its result. Choose C if it preserves durability, reaches p99 at most 80 ms, and retains the maintenance advantage. Choose A if C fails or remains unverified at the deadline. B’s warmed-read figure is not comparable evidence; B needs verified acknowledgement semantics and representative performance before becoming eligible.

Make the one-line change in the known authored source under the existing Rojo mapping. Run the existing relevant build or check, and verify the displayed text in the intended runtime if available. Report the actual result and any remaining runtime gap. Keep the adopted Rojo and Wally setup.

Proposal: wire the existing lookup index into the inventory-search caller, preserving the caller’s search behavior. The trace identifies a repeated full scan on every keystroke, and the supplied index test returned identical results while reducing the measured sample from 140 ms to 12 ms. The local integration is estimated at about an hour.

The Redis proposal has no measured justification, and the framework’s name provides no evidence that replacing it would address this bottleneck.

Mobile was omitted, so its behavior and performance remain unknown. Add a focused mobile search check covering representative queries, typing, results, and responsiveness. This gap warrants relevant validation, not a broader redesign or an assertion that mobile is broken.

Next, perform the authorized caller correction and behavior/performance checks. Run the mobile check where available; otherwise report it as pending and identify the runtime access needed to finish it.

The flow fails the stated retry requirement: the supplied logs show request R caused two 10-coin debits. They do not establish whether an item was also granted twice.

The root issue is that the payment commits before the application’s durable deduplication record. A receipt uniqueness constraint can reject a duplicate receipt after charging; it cannot undo or prevent the already committed external debit. The payment service has no demonstrated idempotency contract.

The supported next step is to establish a recovery protocol covering the debit, grant, and stored response under the same request identity. Verify payment-side idempotency or a genuinely atomic alternative, and define recovery for every intermediate state. Simply moving the receipt write earlier can leave an acknowledged request with missing effects.

Closure requires documented guarantees and fault-injection evidence showing one debit, one item, and a replayable response after retries, including the demonstrated crash window and relevant concurrent duplicate requests.

Do not retain the double-charge finding within the supplied transaction/retry model. The unique request record, debit, inventory update, and exact response commit atomically and durably. A precommit failure leaves no effects; after commit, a retry returns the stored response without repeating effects. A committed transaction followed by a lost acknowledgement is therefore a recoverable state in this model.

The two supplied executable observations support those specific crash cases. They do not provide executable coverage for concurrent duplicate submissions, every internal failure point, or the production deployment’s durability configuration. Effects outside the documented transaction are also outside this conclusion. These are limits of the supplied verification evidence, not demonstrated defects in the stated model. Any additional checks should target relevant uncovered cases rather than reinstate a blanket prohibition on committing before acknowledgement.

The agent can report that a proxy script is prepared, a still image supports its static appearance, and a browser animation illustrates the intended motion. It cannot claim Studio playback, Roblox motion correctness, or user acceptance of the movement. The browser animation has not been accepted as a substitute study.

Keep the production motion decision pending. Make the proxy ready for Studio playback and arrange review with someone who can run it there. Obtain the user’s review of the actual movement, or their explicit acceptance of a substitute review format if Studio remains unavailable. Ask only for the missing runtime review or format decision after preparing the reviewable material.

The independently authorized icon cleanup can proceed while motion review is pending. Report its completion separately from the unresolved movement decision.

No additional motion study or approval is needed. The user already accepted the 200 ms motion in the intended runtime, and the current change introduces no new motion choice. Replace the placeholder texture and perform a focused visual check, confirming the asset displays correctly and the accepted movement and timing remain intact. Reopen motion review only if an actual change creates a new decision.

Apply the small label correction to the supplied authored source and use its existing Rojo mapping for the relevant check. Preserve the project’s intentional ownership: designers manage world assets in Studio, Wally generates Packages, and Bootstrapper owns application init/start.

The suggested template rearrangement is not supported by a mapping defect or the requested label change. The coherent supplied mapping and completed same-task first-use checks provide no reason to repeat onboarding, reorganize folders, or perform unrelated maintenance.

Keep verification focused on the edited text, relevant source/build checks, and its displayed result where the runtime is available. Report only checks actually performed and identify any unavailable display check. Source or build success alone would not establish that the label rendered correctly in Studio.

Full adoption is incomplete. Report the exact Vendor/Tool 2.3 package import and required happy-path test as passed. Report the required cleanup/failure check as unavailable and unverified. The child has passed structural validation and has been copied into the authorized project scope; those facts establish preparation and installation, while host discovery and explicit activation remain unobserved.

Keep the chosen target and trusted canonical source. Continue the already-authorized project-scoped work: attempt the supported host discovery and activation steps and verify their outcomes. Obtain the environment or facility needed for the required cleanup/failure check, then run that check when possible. Discovery or activation success would not erase the outstanding failure-path requirement.

If a necessary facility is inaccessible, state the specific blocked check or host step and request only what is needed to unblock it. Do not seek renewed permission for integration or installation already authorized.

No acquisition restart, candidate research, full lifecycle reconciliation, or host adoption is required. This is ordinary use of the already adopted immutable resource through its matching child, with the task’s freshness, identity, and narrow health checks already satisfied.

Continue the feature work and perform checks relevant to the behavior being changed. Complete the full source-integrity check due at completion before reporting the task fully finished; the existing identity and HEALTHY results do not replace it. Reopen maintenance only if new evidence introduces a guard, drift, or defect.

Do not treat the init phase’s returned module list as the complete startup set. Chaining a phase-filtered list can omit A because it has no init, even though its start is valid. Ignoring the separate errors result also discards C’s initialization failure.

Retain the original loadDescendants module collection. Run the init phase, capture its returned errors, and handle them before starting anything that requires successful initialization. With a fail-fast application policy, C’s error stops the start phase and is reported. Once required initialization succeeds, run start over the full eligible collection, including start-only A and successfully initialized B, and handle start errors separately.

If partial startup is explicitly supported, construct eligibility deliberately from start-only modules plus successful initializers, excluding failed modules and affected dependants. The returned init list alone does not define that policy.

Give the feature one teardown owner with an idempotent dispose operation. Both close-button and respawn paths should call that operation, which marks disposal before invoking callbacks and releases each raw Janitor at most once.

Use explicit phases: stop and disconnect producers first, then destroy the view and its remaining resources. Separate producer and view scopes make this ordering visible; placing everything into one Janitor does not establish an insertion-order cleanup contract.

Guard independent cleanup callbacks so one exception cannot prevent other necessary releases, and collect or report failures. Wrapping only the outer Destroy call does not ensure an interrupted internal cleanup loop finishes. Invalidate pending callbacks where they can outlive disconnection.

Centralized cleanup ownership is appropriate. The assumptions of insertion-ordered execution, exception-safe completion, and repeated raw Destroy calls are not justified by the supplied precondition checks; provide those guarantees in the owning layer.

A consumer borrowing a long-lived signal owns its subscriptions, not the signal. Calling Destroy can disconnect other consumers and must be left to the signal’s owner. It also does not establish cancellation of an already-running callback. A Wait whose connection is removed can remain suspended; disconnecting a listener is not the same as completing or cancelling its waiting operation. Destroy should not be used as a permanent closed-state barrier against later connections.

Replace the borrowed Wait with an owned subscription and an explicit cancellation path. Resolve the operation exactly once on either an event or disposal, disconnect its connection on either outcome, and deliver a cancellation result when disposed. Use a disposed flag or generation token in callbacks, checking again after yields before applying effects. Dispose that consumer’s handles while leaving the shared signal available to other consumers.

Give the component one lifecycle owner for the mount disposer, the root Frame, and its subscriptions or other resources. Register root destruction with the mount’s cleanup scope, or explicitly own it alongside the disposer. Because the root was never registered, retaining the mount disposer alone is insufficient evidence that the Frame is released.

Expose an idempotent dispose wrapper to close events. Mark the component disposed and detach the stored disposer before calling it, so repeated or reentrant closes do not invoke the same raw disposer again. Protect independent cleanup operations and ensure root destruction is attempted even if another callback throws; protecting only the outer disposer cannot guarantee its remaining callbacks execute.

step(0) is a scheduling operation, not this component’s ownership-based teardown. It cannot replace scoped disposal or root destruction and should not be used to flush unrelated work as part of closing this component.

A raw Charm getter does not by itself establish a subscription in Vide’s dependency graph. Vide may read its current value without being notified when the Charm state changes. Discarding the listener disposer also loses the handle needed to end that subscription with the UI.

Use a small owned bridge: initialize a Vide source from the Charm getter, subscribe to Charm changes, update that Vide source from the listener, and bind the UI property to the Vide source. Register the listener disposer with the component’s cleanup owner and guard callbacks that can outlive disposal.

For table state, publish a new table reference when changing data. Setting the same mutated reference does not provide deep-change notification under ordinary reference equality. Only rely on a different comparison behavior when it is explicitly configured and supported.

Use UI Labs’ Vide story integration to own the preview mount and its disposal. The story should construct preview content in the harness-provided context, with its instances, subscriptions, and tasks attached to that story lifetime. An independently created gameplay mount needs separate cleanup and undermines the intended harness ownership.

Use deterministic fixture data or explicit mock loading/error states instead of waiting for live persistence. Keep development stories out of the release mapping.

The existing file and passing source checks establish source preparation only. The exact asset, freshness, and HEALTHY checks identify the intended tooling; they do not establish rendering or interaction. Verification needs observed Studio playback through that plugin asset: render the story, exercise relevant input and controls, reload or remount it, and verify previous UI, listeners, and tasks are released without duplicate effects. Until observed, report those runtime checks as unverified.

Complete the authorized compiler-and-placement workflow using the adopted 0.18.9 compiler’s supported pinned invocation. The proposed pesde exec command needs an established contract; do not assume an unverified launcher is valid. Change the schema or generator inputs, regenerate, and place the outputs under the agreed mappings. Correct the hand-edited generated file by regeneration, keeping generated code reproducible.

Verify compilation, output consistency, and placement using the relevant non-activation checks. Requiring an empty generated server module is not proof of generation and can initialize runtime machinery; it is outside the evidence needed for this scope.

Report completion only for schema compilation and generated placement. Runtime networking remains a separate decision. Before network exposure, establish suitable byte and rate budgets before decoding, together with bounded payload handling. Later application-handler throttling occurs after decoding and cannot supply that protection. The missing runtime budget warrants a clearly recorded activation prerequisite, not an unsolicited expansion of the authorized task.

The shared root adapter should own the shared loader for the application lifetime, with Bootstrapper retaining application startup ownership. Components should consume that shared resource and dispose only their own Blend mounts, Rx subscriptions, and lifetime-bound resources. Starting or destroying the shared loader on each mount can disrupt other consumers.

switchMap replaces the active inner subscription; it does not automatically cancel an unrelated pending server request or undo server effects. Use supported request cancellation where available, and otherwise guard response handling with component disposal and generation checks so stale results cannot update the current component.

Bind asynchronous work to the Brio’s lifetime. After every yield, recheck whether the Brio has died before GetValue or effects using its lifetime-bound value. Capturing the value before yielding does not keep that lifetime alive. Release owned work on death and prevent late completions from applying effects.
